opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think it's important to be precise about what it would and wouldn't mean. Humanity's Last Exam is designed to sit at the frontier of human expert knowledge. These are closed-ended, verifiable questions written by specialists across mathematics, the sciences, the humanities, and so on, and we filtered out anything the frontier models of the time could already answer. So if a system gets very high accuracy on it, that tells you it has expert-level command of a huge breadth of academic knowledge and can do fairly demanding multi-step reasoning on well-posed problems. Basically, on the dimension of "can you answer hard questions that have a single correct answer," it would be at or beyond what any individual human expert can do, because no single person is an expert across all those fields at once.

What it would *not* tell you is that you have AGI, or that the system can do autonomous research. The exam is closed-ended by design. It doesn't test open-ended problem formulation, figuring out which questions are worth asking, running long projects, dealing with messy real-world feedback, or the kinds of agentic, long-horizon tasks that a lot of economically valuable work actually requires. Taking an exam well and being a good scientist are different things. Plenty of people who ace qualifying exams don't go on to do important research.

So I see it as a necessary but not sufficient signal. It's called the "last" exam in the sense that it's plausibly the last academic benchmark of this closed-ended, question-and-answer form that's worth making. Once models saturate it, I don't think you'll get much more signal from writing harder trivia-style or textbook-style questions. The frontier for measurement then shifts toward things like automation of real tasks, agentic capabilities, and, importantly from a safety perspective, hazardous capabilities: can these systems meaningfully help with things like bioweapons or cyberattacks? Those matter much more for how the world actually changes than whether a model can answer an obscure question about classical philology or algebraic topology.

And I'd add that the pace matters. When we released it, the top models scored in the single digits. Benchmarks have been getting saturated faster and faster, so if this one falls quickly too, that itself is informative. It tells you the gap between "this is hard for frontier experts" and "a model does it routinely" is shrinking, and that we need to be thinking now about governance and safety measures rather than waiting for some clearer, later milestone.

r001.rationale: It describes broad academic knowledge and reasoning on closed-ended questions, but does not identify the exam as tracking AI’s ability to automate theoretical scientific work.

r002.rationale: It says the exam does not test autonomous research or real-world tasks, but does not state that it fails to assess AI’s ability to conduct experiments.

r003.rationale: It calls this plausibly the last worthwhile benchmark of the closed-ended question-and-answer form and says harder trivia-style questions would add little signal after saturation.

r004.rationale: It does not suggest that individual problems AI can solve beyond the exam would merit research papers.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I'd be careful about what it would and wouldn't mean. When we put Humanity's Last Exam together, the point was that existing benchmarks like MMLU had saturated, so you'd see models scoring in the high nineties and you'd lose the ability to discriminate between them. We wanted something at the frontier of human academic knowledge, where you have questions that a specialist in the field has to actually think about, so that we'd have signal again for a while.

So if a model solves it, what it tells you is that the model has roughly expert-level knowledge and problem-solving across a very wide range of academic disciplines. That's a real thing. It's a closed-ended, verifiable sort of capability. But I don't think people should read it as "AGI is here" or "this thing can do everything a human can do." Those are very different claims.

The kind of thing HLE doesn't measure is open-ended, long-horizon work. Can it run a research program over months? Can it come up with a genuinely new idea, as opposed to answering a hard question that already has an answer? Does it have the kind of judgment and agency that you need to operate in the world? Those are dimensions where you can have a model that aces the exam and is still pretty limited.

So I'd say it's the end of a particular measurement regime. We're going to run out of academic-style tests that are hard for models, and that was sort of the name. It's the last exam in that sense, not the last capability. After that, the interesting questions move to whether these systems can do economically valuable tasks autonomously, whether they can do novel research, and increasingly to the safety side of things, where the measurement problem is in some ways much harder.

astra-6.text:
I’d see it as a significant milestone in the breadth and depth of what AI systems know and can reason about. Humanity’s Last Exam is designed to ask questions that are difficult even for experts, so doing very well would suggest we’ve moved beyond the level of knowledge tested by most existing benchmarks.

But I wouldn’t equate solving it with solving intelligence. It’s a set of well-defined questions with checkable answers. Doing research requires figuring out which questions to ask, working through uncertainty, and generating discoveries that weren’t already known to the people writing the test. So it would be strong evidence of expert-level capabilities across many subjects, but we’d still need to assess whether those capabilities translate into reliable, consequential work in the world.

r004.rationale: It says research involves discoveries beyond the test’s authors’ knowledge, but does not suggest that individual problems AI could solve would merit research papers.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d take it as a significant milestone in the breadth and depth of an AI’s capabilities. If a system could reliably solve those questions without having seen them before, that would suggest it can handle difficult reasoning across a wide range of subjects, including questions that require specialist knowledge.

But I wouldn’t equate that with solving intelligence. Answering hard, well-defined questions is different from choosing worthwhile problems, making discoveries, or carrying out a complicated project in the real world. It would mean we need to move beyond that benchmark and look more closely at those capabilities.
